To pester someone means to repeatedly bother or annoy them — usually by constantly asking for something, making demands, or interrupting them — in a way they find irritating and unwelcome. The person being pestered typically wants to be left alone, but the other person just won't stop.

Think of a child in a supermarket who keeps asking their parent, "Can I have candy? Can I have candy? Please? Please? Please?" — even after being told "no" multiple times. That child is pestering the parent.

To truly understand this word, you need to see that it always carries three ideas together:

1. Repetition — It is never a one-time action. You pester someone by doing something again and again. If you ask once and stop, that is not pestering.

2. Persistence — The person keeps going even after being ignored, told to stop, or shown that their behaviour is unwelcome. They do not take the hint.

3. Annoyance — The person on the receiving end feels irritated, bothered, and frustrated. Their peace is disturbed.

If any one of these three is missing, the word "pester" may not be the right fit.
What Is Usually "Done" When You Pester Someone?

Pestering almost always involves one of these actions repeated over and over:

  • Asking for something (a favour, a gift, money, attention, an answer)
  • Making a request or a demand
  • Interrupting someone who is busy
  • Pushing someone to do something they haven't agreed to

"Pester" sits at a mild-to-moderate level of bothering someone. It is more than a tiny, one-time inconvenience, but it is not as serious or aggressive as words like harass or torment. It describes behaviour that is annoying and tiresome, not threatening or dangerous.

Imagine a fly that keeps landing on your arm. It is not hurting you, but it won't leave you alone — that persistent, low-level irritation is the feeling "pester" captures perfectly.
How "Pester" Is Used in Sentences (Grammar Patterns)

There are three very common patterns:

Pattern 1: pester + person + for + something
This is used when someone keeps asking for a specific thing.

  • She pestered her father for a new bicycle for weeks.
  • He kept pestering the waiter for more bread.

Pattern 2: pester + person + to + do something
This is used when someone keeps pushing another person to take an action.

  • My friends pestered me to join their team.
  • She pestered her doctor to run more tests.

Pattern 3: pester + person + with + something
This is used when someone keeps troubling another person by throwing something at them repeatedly — often questions, calls, or messages.

  • He pestered me with phone calls all afternoon.
  • The journalist pestered the politician with the same question over and over.

• At home: A younger sibling pestering an older one to play a game when the older one is trying to study.
  • At work: An employee pestering their manager every single day for a salary raise before the manager has had time to think about it.
  • In sales: A salesperson pestering a potential customer with daily emails and calls even after the customer has shown no interest.
  • Among friends: A friend pestering you to come to a party after you have already said you are busy.
  • Online: Someone pestering a celebrity on social media by commenting on every post and sending repeated messages.
How "Pester" Feels — The Tone of the Word

"Pester" is a slightly informal word. It is perfectly fine to use in everyday conversation, casual writing, and most standard writing. It would be unusual in very formal legal or academic writing, where words like "harass" or "repeatedly solicit" might be preferred.

The word often carries a slightly judgmental tone toward the person doing the pestering. When you say "she pestered him," you are gently criticising her behaviour — suggesting she was being unreasonable, childish, or simply too much. It is not a neutral word.

Bother — A broader, gentler word. You can bother someone just once, by accident, without being persistent. Pester is always deliberate and repeated.

Annoy — This describes the feeling caused in the other person. Pester describes the action being done. Someone can annoy you without pestering you (for example, by chewing loudly). And pestering causes annoyance — but the word "pester" focuses on the repeated bothering, not the emotional result.

Nag — Very close to pester, but "nag" usually happens inside a close relationship (a partner, a parent, a spouse) and often involves repeatedly reminding or complaining about duties or responsibilities. Pester is broader and can happen between strangers.

Badger — Similar to pester, but slightly stronger and more forceful. To badger someone implies more aggressive, relentless pressure to get them to do something or change their mind. Pestering is more about being a nuisance; badgering is more about wearing someone down.

Harass — Much stronger and more serious. Harassment implies deliberate, ongoing behaviour intended to intimidate, harm, or distress someone, and often has legal consequences. Pestering is annoying; harassment is harmful.

• It does not mean to physically hurt or threaten someone.
  • It does not mean to bother someone just once.
  • It does not mean to accidentally disturb someone.
  • It does not carry a meaning of violence or aggression.

Before you use "pester," ask yourself three questions:

  1. Is the action being repeated — not just done once? ✅
  2. Is the person continuing despite being unwelcome? ✅
  3. Is the person on the receiving end feeling annoyed or disturbed? ✅

If all three answers are yes, "pester" is likely the right word.
